ratings_why.fun: Every buff becomes a 'who is she on?' question, and watching a hub and its vines grow together is a real joy, though the rule load and daily re-hanging cost some ease.
ratings_why.distinct: Over a 7 because one rule ('gains stats no other way') turns every buff in the lobby, even other tribes' engines, into a placement puzzle, and units that live and die with their host; no current tribe plays like that.

verdict_why: The core reads well and the fantasy lands; Ruin Ivy and Viscum need clearer wording before the design settles.

points.text: Ruin Ivy's '(Rising is unaffected)' can be read two ways: do the host's Climbers then rise from the redirected stats or not? Say it plainly, e.g. 'Its Climbers then rise from it as normal.'

Viscum's 'also rise with each of your other hosts' is hard to picture: does a Climber copy gains from hosts across the board, and does Grand Oak's doubling apply? Name what a Climber copies, e.g. 'copies the gains of every host you have, not just its own.'

The fantasy comes through in play, not just names: dodder gatecrashing the enemy's biggest unit, the thrush catching falling Climbers, the dowager's guest-book of hosts. Keep that card-by-card tie when revising.
Hazel Wand says 'for each Climber on it' but holds one unless Hop Bine is out, so the text promises more than it usually does. Giving it Hold 2 would make the line read true from turn 2.
Ivy Solicitor's exception line is the one rule a player must remember mid-turn; a cleaner shape is 'give its host that Climber's stats permanently; this gain isn't copied.'

standouts.why: Cousin Dodder reads at a glance and is pure character: he latches onto their biggest unit and his fall feeds you.
Missel catching the Climbers of a dying host is the thrush guarding his berries, and it answers the tribe's main fear in one line.
The Grand Oak is the obvious, readable goal of the tribe: the fashionable address everyone wants to climb.

weakest.why: Viscum's effect is the hardest to read in the set and its character (old blood, Pliny) doesn't show in what it does.
Ruin Ivy's redirect and its parenthesis need a second read, and the card reads as rules plumbing rather than an ivy-clad ruin.
Ivy Solicitor works on paper but adds an exception players must hold in their head.

flags.note: Which hosts' gains each Climber copies, and how it stacks with the Grand Oak, isn't clear from the text.
Whether Climbers rise from the redirected stats is ambiguous.
With Kissing Bough and several hosts, every hosted Climber copies every host's gain each turn; worth the owner's eye.
A golden Oak with Hop Bine and four Climbers is the design's own named high roll.
